title: The Funeral Home Called Me Eight Days After My Mother Died to Say Her $11,400 Prepaid Funeral Plan Had Been Cancelled in 2020, and With a $13,900 Bill Due by Friday, I Learned One Sister Had Signed the Cancellation, the Other Had Cashed the
excerpt: The funeral home called me eight days after my mother died to say her prepaid funeral plan had been cancelled in 2020.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — Eight Days
The funeral home called me eight days after my mother died to say her prepaid funeral plan had been cancelled in 2020.

I was standing in my kitchen in Newark, Ohio, writing thank-you notes for casseroles. My mother, Margaret Doyle, had passed the previous Tuesday at eighty-four, three years after a second stroke took most of her speech but none of her stubbornness. We had been planning her funeral around the plan she bought herself in 2014.
“Mrs. Kaminski,” the funeral director said gently, “I’m afraid there’s a problem with your mother’s arrangements. Could you come in this afternoon?”

His name was Mr. Holloway. He had run Holloway & Sons Funeral Home on Church Street for thirty-one years, and his father before him. He had buried my father in 2009. He was the kind of man who remembered your children’s names.
In his office, he slid a copy of a document across his polished desk.
“Cancellation of Preneed Funeral Contract.” Dated August 2020. It requested cancellation of my mother’s plan and a refund of all funds paid.
“The full amount was refunded,” Mr. Holloway said quietly. “Eleven thousand, four hundred dollars.”
“That’s impossible,” I said. “Mom bought that plan so none of us would ever have to pay for her funeral. She showed me the paperwork herself. She was proud of it. She had it framed, practically.”
I remember the day she showed me. She had the folder out on her kitchen table, with her reading glasses on the end of her nose. “There,” she’d said. “Now you girls won’t have to fight over a casket.”
Mr. Holloway slid a second document across the desk. A copy of the refund check, front and back.

It had been made out to Margaret Doyle and mailed to her house on Hudson Avenue. On the back was Mom’s endorsement, in a shaky signature that looked like hers after her first stroke. And under it: “Pay to the order of Linda Doyle Ferris.”
It had been deposited at a bank branch in Columbus.
“Mom never lived in Columbus,” I said. “She never had an account there.”
“I understand,” Mr. Holloway said. “But your sister Linda does.”
I’m fifty-eight. I have two younger sisters. Linda is the youngest. She lives in Columbus.
Now the funeral would cost $13,900, Mom had been dead for eight days, and we had to decide by Friday.
PART 2 — Three Sisters

My mother raised three daughters in a narrow white house on Hudson Avenue, on a high school secretary’s salary and my father’s paycheck from the glass plant. I’m the oldest, Theresa. Paula is fifty-five. Linda is fifty-one.

We were close growing up, the way sisters are when they share one bathroom. We fought over the hair dryer and the phone cord and who got the front seat. But we always closed ranks when anyone else came after one of us.

After Mom’s stroke in 2019, the three of us agreed to take turns handling her affairs. Each of us would serve a year as her financial power of attorney, paying her bills and managing her accounts, so no one carried the whole burden. I did 2019. Paula did 2020. Linda did 2021. Then I took over again.
It worked. Mostly. We kept a shared spreadsheet. We met at Mom’s house once a month.
I thought we told each other everything. I thought we didn’t have secrets anymore.
I called Paula from the funeral home parking lot.
She answered on the second ring. “Hey, I was just going to call you about the flowers…”
“Paula,” I said, “the funeral home says Mom’s prepaid plan was cancelled in August 2020. While you had power of attorney.”
Then my sister started to cry. Not dramatic crying. Quiet, as if she’d been holding it for four years.
“I can explain,” she said. “But not on the phone.”
“Paula, the refund check was signed over to Linda. She cashed it in Columbus.”
“I know,” Paula whispered. “And Linda can’t know.”
“Linda can’t know what? She’s the one who cashed it.”
“She doesn’t know where it came from,” Paula said. “Please, Theresa. Come over tonight. I’ll tell you everything. And then you decide.”
PART 3 — Paula’s Kitchen

Paula lives in Heath, ten minutes from me, in a split-level with a basketball hoop that her sons haven’t used in a decade. When I walked into her kitchen that night, she had a folder on the table and two cups of tea she had made and forgotten to drink.
“Do you remember the summer of 2020?” she asked.
Of course I did. Everyone does. The pandemic. Masks. Empty grocery store shelves. Mom alone in her house on Hudson Avenue because we were afraid to visit and bring her the virus.
“Do you remember Linda that summer?” Paula asked.
I thought about it. Linda had been quiet. She’d skipped our video calls a few times. She said work was busy. Her husband, Greg, had been laid off from his restaurant job in March. I knew that much.
“I knew Greg lost his job,” I said. “I thought they were managing.”

“They weren’t,” Paula said. “They were four months behind on rent. Their landlord had filed for eviction.” The court was about to set a date. Linda had three kids still at home. She was too proud to tell any of us.”
I stared at her. In 2020, Mom could barely speak a full sentence. After her second stroke, she communicated mostly with a whiteboard and a lot of very expressive eyebrows.

“Linda called Mom every night that summer,” Paula said. “Mom couldn’t say much, but she could listen. Linda told her everything. Things she wouldn’t tell us. One night in July, Mom wrote on her whiteboard and held it up to the camera when I was visiting.”
Paula opened the folder and took out a photograph she had taken on her phone and printed. It showed Mom’s little whiteboard, in Mom’s shaky marker handwriting.
PART 4 — Mom’s Orders
I sat at Paula’s kitchen table and stared at the photograph for a long time.
“I told her no,” Paula said. “I said, ‘Mom, you paid for that so we wouldn’t have to. If we cancel it, who pays for your funeral?’ She just tapped the whiteboard. Over and over. ‘GIVE IT TO LINDA.’”

“Not right away,” Paula said. “I called Mom’s lawyer, Mr. Stanek. He came to the house with a mask on and sat with her for an hour. He asked her questions. She answered them, yes and no, nodding and shaking her head. He said she understood exactly what she was asking.”

Paula took out another document. A short statement from Mr. Stanek, dated July 2020, saying that Margaret Doyle had clearly expressed her wish to cancel her preneed funeral contract and direct the refund to her daughter Linda, and that in his opinion she was competent to make that decision.
“In Ohio,” Paula said, “a prepaid funeral contract can be cancelled. Mom had a revocable plan. The funeral home had to refund what she’d paid in.”
“The funeral home mailed it to Mom. I helped her endorse it. Her hand was shaking so badly it took three tries.” Paula wiped her eyes. “Then she wrote on her whiteboard again.”
“DON’T TELL LINDA IT WAS MY FUNERAL. TELL HER IT’S FROM MY SAVINGS.”

“Mom didn’t want Linda to feel guilty,” Paula said. “She said Linda would never take it if she knew. So I drove it to Columbus myself. I told Linda Mom wanted her to have it from her savings. She cried and cried. She paid the landlord the next day. They kept the apartment.”
“Why didn’t you tell me?” I asked. “I was the next power of attorney after you.”
Paula looked down. “Because Mom made me promise. And because you would have told Linda. You always do.”
PART 5 — What Friday Meant
On the drive home, I tried to think about Friday.

Mr. Holloway had been as gentle as a man could be. But funerals cost what they cost. The casket Mom had chosen, the visitation, the Mass at Blessed Sacrament, the burial next to Dad at Cedar Hill Cemetery. $13,900. He needed a signed contract and a deposit by Friday to hold the church and the cemetery crew.
I had about $6,000 in savings. My husband Rick and I were still paying for our youngest son’s last year at Ohio State.
